title: Counsel Defeated: Hushai, Ahithophel, and David's Escape
summary: Ahithophel advises Absalom to strike David at once with twelve thousand men and kill only the king. Hushai counters with a flattering, slower plan: gather all Israel and let Absalom lead them himself. Absalom chooses Hushai's advice, because the LORD had purposed to defeat Ahithophel's good counsel. Warned by the priests' sons, who hide in a well to escape capture, David crosses the Jordan to Mahanaim, where loyal friends east of the Jordan bring food and supplies. Ahithophel, seeing his advice rejected, goes home and takes his own life.
story: This is the hinge of Absalom's rebellion. At the end of chapter 15 David prayed that God would turn Ahithophel's counsel to foolishness and then sent Hushai back to the city. Here the prayer is answered. Ahithophel's plan was sound and would probably have ended David's life; Hushai's buys time, and time is what David needs. The narrator steps in with one of the clearest theological comments in the book (verse 14) to say that God was at work in a political debate. From here the rebellion moves toward the battle in chapter 18. The chapter also shows David's support in the lands east of the Jordan, where kindness he showed years before is repaid.
historical:
Mahanaim, east of the Jordan in Gilead, had been the capital of Saul's son Ish-bosheth after Saul's death (2:8-9), and it was a fortified town where David could regroup. Its name recalls Jacob, who met angels there (Genesis 32:1-2). The men who bring supplies in verses 27-29 represent different peoples of the region: Shobi son of Nahash, from the Ammonite capital Rabbah (probably a brother of Hanun, whom David had fought in chapters 10-12, and perhaps now ruling there under David); Machir from Lo-debar, who had sheltered Mephibosheth (9:4); and the wealthy Barzillai of Gilead, who will reappear in chapter 19.

Amasa, Absalom's new commander, was related to both David and Joab. According to 1 Chronicles 2:16-17, Abigail and Zeruiah were David's sisters, so Amasa and Joab were cousins and David's nephews. The mention here of Abigail as “the daughter of Nahash” is a puzzle; some think Nahash was the name of her mother or of an earlier husband of David's mother. The father's description also varies between the Hebrew texts of Samuel and Chronicles (Israelite or Ishmaelite), and the BSB follows Chronicles.
cultural:
Counsel in an ancient royal court was a formal activity. Kings consulted advisers before a campaign, and the advice of senior counselors could be decisive. Ahithophel's plan is sound military strategy: strike quickly while the enemy is weary and scattered, kill the leader, and spare the people. Hushai's counter-plan appeals to Absalom's vanity and fear with vivid images: a bear robbed of her cubs, the heart of a lion melting, an army like the sand of the seashore, a city dragged into the valley with ropes. It flatters Absalom with the picture of himself leading all Israel.

The hiding of the messengers in a well recalls Rahab hiding the spies (Joshua 2). Wells and cisterns in courtyards were common, since households depended on stored rainwater. Spreading grain to dry on a cloth was ordinary work that would not draw attention. The supplies brought to Mahanaim (beds, basins, pottery, grains, beans, lentils, honey, curds, sheep, and cheese) were a lavish gift of hospitality to a king in exile.
literary: The chapter's first half is a contest of speeches. Ahithophel's advice is brief and precise; Hushai's is long, rhetorical, and full of images. The narrator marks the verdict in verse 14 with an unusual direct comment: “For the LORD had purposed to thwart the good counsel of Ahithophel in order to bring disaster on Absalom.” It is one of only a few places in the long story of David's family (chapters 9-20) where the narrator says outright what God is doing (compare 11:27 and 12:24). The second half moves quickly: messages, a narrow escape, a crossing by night. Ahithophel's end is told in a single sentence, and the chapter closes with a list of gifts that answers the people's hunger, exhaustion, and thirst.

outline.t: The warning reaches David, and he crosses the Jordan
Absalom pursues with Amasa as commander

doctrines.note: Verse 14 is the chapter's key: God is at work in a political council, turning the better advice aside to accomplish his purpose. He works through human decisions, not around them. Absalom freely chooses, and yet God's purpose stands.

David's prayer in 15:31 that Ahithophel's counsel would be turned into foolishness is answered here. God used Hushai, whom David had sent, to answer the prayer, showing how God often answers through the means people put in place.

Ahithophel's counsel was good by human standards, yet it failed because it stood against God's purpose. Proverbs states the principle: there is no wisdom or counsel that can succeed against the LORD (Proverbs 21:30).

words.note: Etsah, counsel or advice. The word runs through the chapter: Ahithophel's counsel, Hushai's counsel, and the LORD's purpose standing over both. The narrator calls Ahithophel's advice good, but good counsel set against God's purpose comes to nothing.

Parar, to break or frustrate. The LORD purposed to thwart Ahithophel's counsel (verse 14). The same verb describes breaking a covenant, and here it describes God breaking a plan. The prophets use it when they say that God frustrates the plans of the nations (Psalm 33:10).

Avar, to pass over or cross. It appears seven times, mostly for crossing the Jordan. David's escape depends on getting across the river before Absalom's army can reach him, and by daybreak no one was left who had not crossed.

Tsavah, to command or ordain. In verse 14 it describes the LORD's decree, which the BSB renders purposed. What looks like a chance preference in Absalom's council was, the narrator says, what God had ordained.

christ: Ahithophel, David's trusted counselor who betrayed him and then took his own life, has long been compared with Judas, the disciple who betrayed Jesus and then hanged himself (Matthew 27:3-5). The comparison is a pattern the Gospel writers' readers noticed, not a prediction in this chapter. The deeper connection is verse 14's picture of God working through human plans. The early church saw the same thing at the cross, praying that the rulers who gathered against Jesus did what God's hand and plan had determined beforehand (Acts 4:27-28). The worst human counsel was overruled to accomplish salvation.

hard.q: How should a reader think about Ahithophel's suicide?
hard.a: The text reports it briefly and without comment. Ahithophel saw that his counsel had been rejected and probably foresaw that Absalom would fail and that he, as a leading traitor, would face death. The narrator neither praises nor condemns the act, and the Bible's few accounts of suicide (Saul, Ahithophel, Zimri, Judas) are all presented as tragic endings to lives that had gone badly wrong. Scripture elsewhere insists that human life belongs to God and that no one is beyond his mercy. Ahithophel's story shows the despair that can follow ruined plans and wounded pride. Readers who find themselves in that kind of darkness should know that the Bible's story does not end in despair, and that help is available: a trusted friend, a pastor, a doctor, or a crisis line (in the United States, calling or texting 988).

questions: The narrator says God thwarted Ahithophel's good counsel. How does believing God works through human decisions affect how you make plans?
Hushai's advice appealed to Absalom's pride. Where are you most vulnerable to advice that flatters you?
Friends from unexpected places supplied David in his need. Who has provided for you in a hard season, and how might you do the same for someone else?
